percentage_note: no percentage was moved by the planning documents or the ADRs. The single change in this snapshot is virtual_memory 45 -> 50: unmapping now returns the frames the space owns (ownership bit), an address space is destroyed with its private chain and its slot, and the slot is reused with a generation; each of those has a host test. The interrupt registry, the single tick source and the capability destruction are recorded as implementation evidence inside their subsystems but did not move the percentage, because their execution paths have never run. scheduler 55 -> 60 in the follow-up of the same day: its policy now runs in the host suite (12 tests) and writing them closed three preemption defects; the lock, the per-CPU ownership and the idle task remain open, so it is not higher. scheduler 60 -> 62 in the third follow-up of the day: the policy moved into a pure module (K3 step 2), a wait queue with deadlines and a mutex with ownership and direct handoff exist with 21 tests, but nothing in the kernel calls them yet and the scheduler still has no lock, which is why the move is two points and not more. scheduler 62 -> 68 in the fourth follow-up of the day: the state lock with per-CPU ownership and the generic blocking primitive exist with host tests (including a four-thread contention test), but no AP has ever run and the mutex has no user in the kernel, so it is not higher.

implemented: CPU table built from the MADT enabled processors (order preserved, duplicates skipped, max_cpus cap)
BSP identified by APIC id; cpuId() translates the local APIC id through the table
AP stacks, trampoline and the INIT-SIPI-SIPI path

the trampoline is copied into the page below 1 MiB that the startup IPI names, with its placement validated against the firmware memory map and its identity mapping installed in the kernel tables (installApTrampoline at boot)

the fields of the block are written in two steps: install (GDT base, far pointer, CR3, EFER bits of the BSP, entry address) and arm (stack and CPU number of one AP, with the ready word cleared before and written last); the offsets come from the symbols of ap_trampoline.s and are validated against the size of the block

one numbering for the CPUs: the index in the CPU table that comes from the MADT indexes the stacks, is passed to the AP in RDI and is what cpuId() returns; a CPU number the table cannot hold is refused before any IPI

the AP sets the EFER bits of the BSP (LME and, when the kernel enabled it, NXE) before it loads the kernel CR3: an NX entry with NXE clear is a reserved bit that faults inside the trampoline, where there is no IDT

an AP that reaches kynox_ap_entry installs its segment, marks itself online and enters the scheduler through a hook (smp.installCpuEntryHook): it adopts a kernel task of its own and gets the idle task of its CPU, so its queue is never empty and current[CPU] is never null
AP startup gated on a published trampoline and on the number of discovered processors, with a bounded wait and explicit failure reporting
limitations: no AP has ever answered a startup IPI in this environment: the copy, the fields and the order are code and host tests, not an observed second processor
an AP that did answer installs its segment, adopts a kernel task and waits with sti; hlt: it takes no task, because nothing wakes it (no reschedule IPI) and it has no clock of its own
the page of the trampoline is checked against the firmware memory map, not against the EBDA pointer at 0x40E

implemented: timer-driven preemption
task contexts and state machine
context-switch assembly
scheduler statistics
one clock counts the tick, so the quantum and the timeout math are no longer doubled by two armed timers
EEVDF choice of the next ready task with a virtual runtime, a deadline and a weight per task
the quantum decides when a task leaves: a tick with slice left only moves the clock
the entering task gets the quantum of its slice, so time-slicing is not a once-per-lifetime event
a preemption that finds no other ready task restores the current one instead of leaving it ready
the scheduler policy covered by host tests (kernel/task_root.zig, artifact scheduler-tests)
the policy is a pure module with no globals (`task/policy.zig`): pickNext, shouldPreempt, quantumFor, budgetFor, minVruntime, tested on their own
a wait queue with FIFO order, a deadline per wait and a remembered wake, so a producer that runs before its waiter cannot lose the wakeup (task/wait.zig)
a mutex with an owner, a recursion limit and a direct handoff: the ownership moves to the waiter before the wake, so no third task can take it in the interval (task/mutex.zig)
the channel of the IPC registers its waiters in the wait queue: the queue has its first caller in the kernel, and the queue of waiters is FIFO instead of being the order of the storage array
a state lock with per-CPU ownership (owner, depth, contentions, re-entries, refused releases) taken by every entry point of the scheduler, released on every path, and counted in the boot report
blockCurrentOn: the generic blocking primitive over any wait queue, with a deadline written before the node is queued and the wait undone when there is nobody to switch to

an idle task created at boot by Scheduler.ensureIdle (idempotent, reported as Statistics.idle): a ring 3 task whose body halts the processor with sti; hlt, with 8 KiB of user stack and 8 KiB of kernel stack

the policy chooses the idle task only when no other task is eligible, whatever its virtual runtime (policy.Entry.idle, policy.idleVruntime), so it is the last resort of the queue and never displaces a real task
one idle task per CPU, with its own user and kernel stacks: the last resort of a processor belongs to that processor

an owner per task (Task.cpu): the choice of a CPU skips every task of another processor, so a second CPU cannot take the task, the stack or the idle task of the first; enqueueReady records the owning CPU

adoptKernelTask: an AP that arrives from the trampoline gets a kernel task of its own (ring 0, its own stack, state running) and becomes current[CPU], so prepareNext has a context to save instead of returning before it reads the queue
limitations: effectively BSP-centric: no AP has ever run, so the lock is never contended in the kernel (it is contended on the host by four threads)
the idle task is created and reported at boot, but no hlt of this tree has executed here
an AP that entered the scheduler sleeps: there is no reschedule IPI and no per-CPU clock, so nothing wakes it with work
the switch to the idle task has never crossed a real context switch (the host tests stop at the decision)
the mutex has no user in the kernel yet; the end-to-end test is the proof of the chain
statisticsOf reads the state without the lock, by design (diagnostics)
no reader/writer lock, no condition variable, no futex-like primitive
no migration or fairness policy, no SMP safety proof
the assembly of the switch still does not save FPU/SSE state (audit defect 8)

Closed for the code: a state lock with per-CPU ownership is taken by every entry point and released on every path (host tests, including four threads contending), the policy is a pure module with its own tests, blockCurrentOn gives the mutex its blocking primitive, the idle task is created at boot and chosen only when nothing else can run, and the segment of the CPU (rsp0, ist1, its own table) is installed by the entry of an AP. Open for the evidence: no AP has ever run, so no two processors contend in the kernel; the trampoline is now published below 1 MiB, INIT/SIPI are sent, the AP enters the scheduler with a task of its own, but no AP has answered and nothing wakes one with work, and the idle task has never halted here

the synchronisation primitives the kernel needs did not exist: no mutex with an owner, no wait queue, and a wait-queue stub whose dequeue returned a field that nothing set. A mutex (owner, recursion, direct handoff) and a wait queue (FIFO, deadlines, remembered wake) now exist with 21 host tests; no kernel path calls them yet

kernel/task/runqueue.zig was a stub that dequeued without shifting and was imported by nothing; deleted. The per-CPU ready queue of the scheduler is the real one, and it is still not safe under SMP because there is no lock

the scheduler called itself inside one decision (tick -> expiry -> wake -> enqueue) with no way to say so, which is why a plain spinlock would have deadlocked on the first tick that expired a wait; the state lock now knows its CPU and counts the re-entries instead. The counters are reported at boot

known_documentation_mismatches: kernel/arch/x86_64/virtio_blk.zig is a legacy stub returning NotImplemented; the active driver is kernel/drivers/kvdi/block.zig. Removal decided in ADR-0003, not executed.
The SDK previously documented ABI level 9 and "no new syscall numbers". Both the SDK and the kernel now alias shared/syscall_abi.zig (revision 1); docs/specs/syscall-abi.md is the reference.
kernel/arch/x86_64/virtio.zig duplicates the split virtqueue that KVDI actually programs, and the boot marker virtio: split queue layout ok currently proves the duplicate (ADR-0002).
kernel/arch/x86_64/virtio_blk.zig used to reference a non-existent docs/adr/ADR-F04-block-driver-proposta.md; corrected. ADRs live in docs/decisions/ per strategy.md.
